target: Frontal EEG Asymmetry (FEA) as a dynamic state-level emotion-regulation signature
note: The paper's core reframing contribution: FEA is not solely a static trait marker of approach/avoidance but also 'a signature of dynamic online emotion regulatory processes' that evolves directionally as situational boredom is coped with and resolved (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., abstract, ~p.8).

target: situational vs. trait/state boredom
note: The paper's entire organizing framework: investigates how trait boredom bears on coping with a state of boredom in real time, operationalizing both a trait level (baseline FEA, self-report scales) and a state level (FEA during peg turning, post-task self-report) (FE, ~p.1).

target: boredom proneness
note: Primary trait dimension given sustained measurement (Boredom Proneness Scale, alpha=.84); the construct most robustly linked to the key finding, inversely predicting FEA slope during peg turning (r=-.48, p<.01) (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5-7).

target: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
note: Central to the interpretive frame: the FEA leftward shift is read as an active regulatory process that emerges over time as boredom ensues, indexing online emotion-regulatory coping (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.6-8).

target: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
note: Present only functionally, never named as such: low-trait-boredom individuals are described as engaging an approach motivation to create stimulation, the paper's closest analogue to an engagement/flow contrast (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.1-2).

target: monotony / meaninglessness
note: The peg-turning task is chosen explicitly for its rated redundancy (most boring of a prior task battery); the Leisure Experience Battery boredom subscale frames leisure boredom as cognitively unsatisfying, meaningless activity (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.4-5).

target: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
note: One item on the post-task Multidimensional State Boredom Scale, 'Time is passing by slower than usual'; not developed into an independent theoretical mechanism (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
note: Mentioned once via a quoted definition of boredom as an aversive state of being unable to attentionally engage (Mercer-Lynn, Bar, & Eastwood, 2014); background framing, not this paper's own operationalized construct (FE, ~p.1).

target: EEG frontal alpha asymmetry
note: Primary DV: natural-log alpha (8-13 Hz) power at F4 minus F3, Laplacian/CSD-transformed; N=51 baseline/N=47 peg-turning; FEA slope during peg turning inversely correlates with boredom proneness (r=-.48, p<.01, d=-1.09) and leisure boredom (r=-.47, p<.01, d=-1.07); no baseline-trait relations (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.4, 6-7).

target: EEG eyes-open vs. eyes-closed
note: Baseline protocol: two alternating 2-min blocks per condition, both included per the rationale (supported by direct citation to Barry et al., 2007) that baseline-FEA correlates are not always observed for both conditions (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.3-4).

target: EEG alpha/theta power
note: Alpha band (8-13 Hz) only, used exclusively to construct the FEA laterality index; no theta power reported or analyzed anywhere in the paper (FE, ~p.4 -- partial/narrow operationalization).

target: self-report / survey scale
note: Four instruments: Boredom Proneness Scale (alpha=.84), Leisure Experience Battery boredom subscale (alpha=.67), Boredom Susceptibility Scale (alpha=.38), Multidimensional State Boredom Scale (alpha=.89) (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: blink / eye-closure
note: ICA-identified blink components removed as an artifact-correction step during EEG preprocessing; not analyzed as a substantive dependent measure of boredom or engagement (FE, ~p.4).

target: boredom proneness <- self-report / survey scale
note: Boredom proneness is operationalized via the 28-item Boredom Proneness Scale (Farmer & Sundberg, 1986), current alpha=.84 (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: situational vs. trait/state boredom <- EEG frontal alpha asymmetry
note: The paper's own construct-measure pairing: the trait/state distinction is operationalized via baseline FEA (trait test, null) vs. FEA slope/intercept during peg turning (state test, supported) (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.6-7).

target: Farmer, Richard, & Sundberg, Norman D. (1986) -- Boredom Proneness Scale
note: Source of the Boredom Proneness Scale, the study's primary trait-boredom instrument (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: Caldwell, Linda L., Smith, Edward A., & Weissinger, Ellen (1992) -- Leisure Experience Battery
note: Source of the leisure-boredom subscale, one of two scales driving the key FEA-slope finding (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: Zuckerman, Marvin (1994) -- Sensation Seeking Scale / Boredom Susceptibility Scale
note: Source of the Boredom Susceptibility Scale, retained despite low reliability (alpha=.38) for its unique relation to approach-oriented traits (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: Fahlman, Shelley A., Mercer-Lynn, Kimberley B., Flora, David B., & Eastwood, John D. (2013) -- Multidimensional State Boredom Scale
note: Source of the 7-item state-boredom manipulation-check instrument administered post-task (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.5).

target: Festinger, Leon, & Carlsmith, James M. (1959)
note: Originators of the peg-turning paradigm adapted as the study's boredom-induction task (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.3-4).

target: Markey, Amanda, Chin, Alycia, Vanepps, Eric M., & Loewenstein, George (2014)
note: Source of the computerized peg-turning adaptation this study models its task on, and of the validation finding that peg turning is rated the most boring of a task battery (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.3-4).

target: Harmon-Jones, Eddie, & Allen, John J. B. (1997)
note: Foundational evidence for FEA covariation with approach/avoidance behavioral sensitivity, underlying the approach-avoidance conceptual model this study relies on (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.2).

target: Tomarken, Andrew J., Davidson, Richard J., & Henriques, Jeffrey B. (1990)
note: Foundational trait-FEA evidence: resting frontal asymmetry predicts affective responses to films (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.2).

target: Choi, Dongwook, Sekiya, Toko, Minote, Naoki, & Watanuki, Shigeki (2016)
note: First of three evidentiary lines motivating the study's hypotheses: reappraisal of negative stimuli is associated with relative greater left frontal activity than mere observation (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.2).

target: Kelley, Nicholas J., Hortensius, Ruud, Schutter, Dennis J. L. R., & Harmon-Jones, Eddie (2017)
note: Second evidentiary line: review of tDCS studies showing induced relative greater/less left frontal activity increases approach-/avoidance-oriented behaviors respectively (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.2).

target: Perez-Edgar, Koraly, Kujawa, Autumn, Nelson, Sara K., Cole, Charlotte, & Zapp, Daniel J. (2013)
note: Third evidentiary line and direct discussion-section parallel: precedent for trait-state FEA interactions emerging under task/stress conditions but not at baseline, mirroring this study's own pattern (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.2, 7).

target: Mercer-Lynn, Kimberley B., Bar, Rachel J., & Eastwood, John D. (2014)
note: Definition of boredom as conflict between aversive attentional disengagement and approach motivation; cited precedent for trait-state boredom interaction in a lab setting (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.1).

target: Weybright, Elizabeth H., Caldwell, Linda L., Ram, Nilam, Smith, Edward A., & Wegner, Lisa (2015)
note: Co-author's own prior work on trait-state boredom interaction with substance use, cited as precedent for the trait-state boredom framework this study extends into neurophysiology (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.1).

target: Zotev, Vadim, et al. (2016)
note: Neurofeedback study shifting frontal activity leftward and reducing depressive symptoms, cited to motivate a future-direction gesture toward boredom-focused neurofeedback intervention (FE, ~p.8-9).

target: Hane, Amie A., & Fox, Nathan A. (2006)
note: Malleability of early approach/avoidance biases based on contextual/caregiving factors, cited for the paper's developmental-origins future-direction gesture (FE, ~p.9).

target: Barry, Robert J., Clarke, Adam R., Johnstone, Stuart J., Magee, Christopher A., & Rushby, Jacqueline A. (2007) -- EEG Differences Between Eyes-Closed and Eyes-Open Resting Conditions
note: Genuine, direct in-text citation (not an inferred cluster link): cited for the premise that lower alpha reflects cortical activation, and to support including both eyes-open and eyes-closed baseline blocks since correlates are not always observed for both. Same-cluster unit bor-sec-27 (Strand D).

target: Fox, Nathan A. (1994) -- dynamic cerebral processes underlying emotion regulation
note: Extends Fox's hemispheric-interplay framework (FEA as dynamic interplay shaped by trait disposition and context) with a novel empirical demonstration of directional evolution over the course of several minutes during a redundant task (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.8).

target: Hewig, Johannes (2018) -- intentionality in frontal asymmetry research
note: Empirically extends Hewig's proposal that FEA reflects the strength of an intention to act (approach or avoidant) even absent overt action, into the novel context of boredom coping (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.2, 7).

target: Coan, James A., Allen, John J. B., & McKnight, Patrick E. (2006) -- capability model
note: Applies and qualifies the capability model to a novel task context (peg turning), evidencing that neural correlates of emotion-regulatory capacity emerge only under active challenge, not at rest, where 'any number of unknown processes are at work' (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.7-8).

target: situational <-> trait framing
note: Reframes the axis by showing trait-boredom individual differences on FEA emerged only at the state/task level (FEA slope during peg turning), not at trait-matched baseline -- evidence that trait dispositions may only become physiologically legible once actively situated in a boring task (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.6-8).

target: self-report <-> physiological-marker as ground truth
note: Reports a genuine dissociation: post-task self-reported state boredom did not correlate with FEA at any point, even though FEA slope tracked trait-boredom self-report scales, cautioning against treating self-report and physiological boredom indices as mutually confirmatory (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.8).

target: EEG frontal-asymmetry-as-boredom-marker <-> confound-with-arousal
note: The source never discusses arousal as a construct or confound -- the word does not occur anywhere in the article -- but performs an analogous specificity check (frontal-vs-parietal control; average-reference robustness) that is the closest it comes to ruling out a generic, non-arousal-specific confound; this characterization of the source's relation to the debate axis is our own (P/anticipatory-application).

target: boredom as unified construct <-> heterogeneous family (within trait boredom)
note: Boredom susceptibility was uncorrelated with the other trait/state scales and its FEA-slope relation did not reach significance despite a similar directional trend, evidencing heterogeneity within trait boredom itself rather than a single unified dimension (FAITHFUL-Perone et al., ~p.6-7).

target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study): EEG frontal alpha asymmetry channel
note: ****** UNVERIFIED: this paper's title and core measure exactly match the controlled measure-axis label 'EEG frontal alpha asymmetry,' and its F3/F4 alpha-band computation plus slope/intercept (RCA) method are directly reusable for any dataset recording repeated-measures frontal EEG across a boredom-inducing session; the dataset entry does not exist on disk, so the match to its actual instrumentation cannot be confirmed (P/anticipatory-application).

target: Part III self-report vs. physiological-index interpretive caution
note: P/anticipatory-application -- the FEA/post-task-self-report dissociation observed here cautions Part III against assuming self-report boredom measures and any future physiological index (via the linked VR Attention Study dataset) would be mutually confirmatory.

target: Part III strata interpretation (lab-VR vs. deployment-2D-PC baseline-vs-task-level effects)
note: P/anticipatory-application -- this study's finding that trait-boredom effects surfaced only at the task/state level, not at baseline, offers Part III a frame for interpreting any null baseline-style individual-difference findings against significant in-task or in-session ones across its desktop-3D vs. video-only strata.

target: Part III repeated/extended-exposure engagement analysis
note: P/anticipatory-application -- the paper's demonstration that FEA shifts directionally over several minutes as task redundancy persists is a candidate physiological analogue for any Part III finding that longer or repeated VLE exposure correlates with increasing self-reported boredom or disengagement.
